sourcedFrom: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) (undated on its face; cached 2026-08-17)
cleanIntro: A hand-fitted 1911, and Ed Brown's maintenance advice is unusual enough that following generic 1911 habits will get it wrong in two directions at once. ⛔ OIL IT HEAVILY — Ed Brown writes that it is impossible to use too much lubrication, and asks for a re-lube every few magazines during a range session, not just at the end. ⛔ AND NO GREASE, of any kind. The tight barrel and slide-to-frame fit that makes the gun shoot is exactly what needs the oil, and grease in those clearances drags. ⚠ Recoil springs are a 3,000-round wear item here and Ed Brown gives the part numbers.

steps.title: Magazine out, hand underneath it
steps.action: Muzzle safe, finger off the trigger, hands away from the muzzle and the ejection port. Put your hand under the magazine so it cannot fall, and press the magazine catch.
steps.prose: Catching the magazine is not neatness — a dropped magazine lands on its feed lips and a bent lip is a stoppage you will spend a range session chasing.
steps.quote: Place your hand under the magazine to prevent it from falling and press the magazine catch to release and eject the magazine.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — UNLOADING, printed p.11

steps.title: Thumb safety DOWN, then rack sharply
steps.action: Press the slide lock safety down out of engagement with the slide, then pull the slide sharply rearward on the cocking serrations to extract and eject whatever is in the chamber.
steps.prose: The thumb safety physically locks the slide on a 1911, so nothing happens until it comes down. Sharply — a slow pull can let a live round slip the extractor and stay in the chamber.
steps.quote: Using the slide cocking serrations, pull slide sharply rearward to extract and eject a round from the chamber.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — UNLOADING, printed p.11

steps.title: Look into the chamber, and look at the magazine well
steps.action: Visually inspect the chamber and confirm the magazine really is out. Then let the slide down onto an empty chamber under control, and squeeze the trigger to lower the hammer.
steps.prose: ⛔ Do not let the slide slam on an empty chamber, here or ever on this pistol. Ed Brown is blunt about the cost: it batters the sear surfaces that were hand-stoned to give the trigger its pull, and it can leave the gun unsafe rather than merely worse.
steps.quote: Visually inspect the chamber to ensure it is empty and the magazine has been removed.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — UNLOADING, printed p.11
steps.warn: Repeatedly allowing the slide to slam closed on a empty chamber will cause premature wear and could damage the finely stoned surfaces of the sear which may ruin the trigger pull or cause an unsafe condition.

steps.title: ⛔ FIRST: does your pistol have a two-piece guide rod?
steps.action: Look at the front of the pistol below the muzzle. If there is a hex-socket screw head in the guide rod, loosen the front end of the guide rod with a 5/32 hex wrench and take it off before anything else. If there is a plain recoil spring plug there instead, skip this and go straight to the slide stop.
steps.prose: ⛔ Ed Brown builds this model both ways, so this is the one thing about your own pistol you have to establish before the strip has a defined order. Trying to push the slide stop out with a two-piece rod still assembled is where people start levering.
steps.aside: NOTE: Safety glasses are recommended, as there are several springs under tension.
steps.quote: For pistols equipped with a two-piece guide rod, loosen the front end of the guide rod with a 5/32 hex head wrench, and remove from gun. If your gun is not equipped with a two-piece guide rod skip to step 2.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — BASIC DISASSEMBLY, printed p.15

steps.title: Align the takedown notch, slide stop out right-to-left
steps.action: Draw the slide back until the slide stop catch lines up with the takedown notch in the slide. Control the top of the gun and push the slide stop pin out from the RIGHT side to the left as far as it will go, then pull it out.
steps.prose: Controlling the top of the gun is the instruction people skip. The slide wants to run forward the moment the stop clears, and on a tightly-fitted gun that is exactly when the pin scrapes a bright arc into the frame.
steps.quote: Pull back on the slide to align the slide stop catch with the takedown notch in the slide. Control the top of the gun while pushing the slide stop pin out as far as possible from right to left, then pull it out completely.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — BASIC DISASSEMBLY, printed p.15

steps.title: ⛔ Hand over the top of the slide, then lift it off
steps.action: Wrap your hand over the top portion of the slide with your fingers across the front, so the recoil spring cannot jump out, and take the slide forward off the frame.
steps.prose: ⛔ On a 1911 with a one-piece plug the spring is genuinely loaded and genuinely leaves. Fingers over the front, every time.
steps.quote: Wrap your hand around the top portion of the slide using your fingers to prevent the recoil spring from jumping out and carefully remove the slide from the frame. CAUTION: the recoil spring is under pressure!
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — BASIC DISASSEMBLY, printed p.15

steps.title: Recoil spring, guide, then the plug
steps.action: Take the recoil spring and the recoil spring guide out, then remove the recoil spring plug from the slide.
steps.prose: Set the frame aside first so you are working on one assembly at a time — the manual says so, and on a bench full of small parts it is the difference between a tidy strip and hunting for a plug.
steps.quote: Carefully remove the recoil spring and recoil spring guide. The recoil spring plug can then be removed from the slide.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — BASIC DISASSEMBLY, printed p.15

steps.title: Bushing counter-clockwise, barrel out the front
steps.action: Turn the barrel bushing fully counter-clockwise, then slide the barrel and bushing out the front of the slide. A bushing wrench if it is tight — and on a hand-fitted gun it usually is.
steps.prose: A match-fitted bushing is meant to be tight. Use the wrench rather than levering with a screwdriver, which is how bushings get scored and stop returning to the same place.
steps.quote: Turn the bushing fully counter-clockwise then slide barrel and bushing out the front of the slide. If necessary, use a bushing wrench.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — BASIC DISASSEMBLY, printed p.15

steps.title: Bore, chamber, breech face, feed ramp
steps.action: Solvent and a bore brush through the barrel from the chamber end, then patches until dry and clean. Carbon off the breech face and around the extractor, and off the barrel hood and locking lugs.
steps.prose: On a .45 ACP the ramp and the chamber mouth are where lead and copper build up, and a tight-chambered match barrel notices it before a loose one does — stiff extraction on a gun that used to extract cleanly is usually this.
steps.quote: Clean and lube the gun after each firing session.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — CLEANING & LUBRICATION, printed p.13

steps.title: ⛔ Lubricate HEAVILY — this is not the usual advice
steps.action: Oil every surface that moves against another one, and concentrate on the barrel fit area — bushing, hood, lower lugs, link — and the slide-to-frame rails.
steps.prose: ⛔ Ed Brown's position is that you cannot over-oil one of these. That is a statement about a hand-fitted gun with tight clearances: the same fit that gives the accuracy is what will gall if it runs dry. It is the opposite of what a polymer striker pistol's manual will tell you, and the difference is the fit, not fashion.
steps.quote: Lube all parts that move against each other, especially in the barrel fit area and slide to frame fit area. It is impossible to use too much lubrication, and we cannot recommend it enough.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — CLEANING & LUBRICATION, printed p.13

steps.title: ⛔ NO GREASE — and re-oil DURING a range session
steps.action: Use oil, not grease, anywhere on this pistol. And if you are shooting a long session, put oil back on the rails and the barrel fit every few magazines rather than waiting until you get home.
steps.prose: ⛔ Both halves are Ed Brown's own instruction and both are unusual enough to be worth stating plainly. Grease of any kind is out; a mid-session re-lube takes seconds and is described as helping ensure flawless functioning.
steps.aside: We recommend lubricating the gun every few magazines during a firing session, if possible.
steps.quote: No grease of any kind is recommended.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — CLEANING & LUBRICATION, printed p.13

steps.title: The Gen4 finish wants a cloth and oil, nothing abrasive
steps.action: Wipe the outside down with a soft cloth lightly wetted with a good gun oil. Nothing abrasive touches the Gen4 finish — no scouring pad, no polishing compound, no wire brush on the flats.
steps.prose: This model ships with that finish by its own model number, SF-G4. It needs no special product, only the discipline not to scrub it.
steps.aside: Do not use anything abrasive on the Gen4 finish.
steps.quote: Our Gen4 finish requires no special care.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — CARE OF GEN4, printed p.14

steps.title: ⛔ Springs are a wear item, and here they are counted
steps.action: Log your round count. Recoil springs get replaced every 3,000 rounds; the firing pin spring and the mainspring every 3,000 to 5,000.
steps.prose: ⛔ This is the maintenance item a 1911 owner most often lets slide, and on a gun with this trigger it shows up as battering rather than as a malfunction. Ed Brown gives the part numbers so there is no guessing about weight.
steps.quote: The firing pin spring (our part number 908) and mainspring (our part number 919) should be replaced every 3,000-5,000 rounds.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — SPRING REPLACEMENT, printed pp.13-15

steps.title: Field strip complete — five pieces and no further
steps.action: Frame, slide, barrel with bushing, recoil spring with its guide, and the recoil spring plug — plus the slide stop and, if fitted, the front half of the guide rod. That is the whole of what Ed Brown publishes for an owner.
steps.prose: ⛔ There is no owner-level extractor, firing pin, sear or grip-safety procedure in this book. Ed Brown's own position on that work is that it belongs to a qualified pistolsmith, and on a gun whose value is in its hand-fitting that is not boilerplate.
steps.quote: Never slam the slide shut without a round being fed from the magazine.
steps.cite: Ed Brown 1911 Owner's Manual — 1911 Owner's Manual (no form or revision code printed) — FUNDAMENTALS OF 1911 HANDLING, printed p.14

deepAbsentReason: ⛔ ED BROWN PUBLISHES NO PROCEDURE PAST THE FIELD STRIP FOR THIS PISTOL, and that is the book's own boundary rather than a gap here. Its contents list runs Basic Disassembly, Alternate Disassembly, Basic Reassembly, Alternate Reassembly and then EVO Series Disassembly and Reassembly — which is a different product line, not a deeper level. There is no owner-level extractor, firing pin, sear, grip safety or mainspring-housing procedure anywhere in it. ⚠ AND ONE TEMPTING SUBSTITUTE WAS REFUSED. The cache also holds Ed Brown's own bench reference (edbrown_bench_reference_2nd.pdf, 168,000 characters), which does cover 1911 pistolsmithing in detail — and its own first page reads "We supply this information for informative purposes only" and recommends that work concerning the safeties or the safe operation of the gun be done by a qualified pistolsmith. A pistolsmithing text is not an owner's deep-clean procedure, and authoring one from it would put bench work behind a cleaning button.

cleaning.name: BARREL & BUSHING
tasks: Solvent and brush from the chamber end, patches until clean
Hood, lower lugs and link wiped and then OILED
Bushing inner face cleaned — it is a bearing surface here

cleaning.name: SLIDE
tasks: Internal rails and the recoil spring tunnel
⛔ Nothing abrasive on the Gen4 exterior

cleaning.name: FRAME
tasks: Rails, disconnector track and the magazine well
⛔ Oil generously — barrel fit and slide-to-frame fit especially

cleaning.name: SPRINGS (round count)
tasks: Firing pin spring and mainspring every 3,000-5,000
5" guns take the 16.5# recoil spring, part number 9165-G

reassembly: Barrel and bushing into the slide from the front, with the link pushed forward.
Turn the bushing so it lines up to accept the recoil spring plug, and make sure the barrel is pushed all the way back so it engages the locking lugs.
Recoil spring plug in from the back, lined up in the bushing.
Recoil spring with its guide attached into the rear of the plug; press the guide into position ahead of the barrel link, rounded cutout against the barrel, link upward.
Hold the spring firmly while the slide goes onto the frame — do not let it jump.

Slide stop pin through the frame AND through the barrel link, resting just below the slide stop plunger; then align the takedown notch and press the slide stop up and IN. ⚠ Push directly in and slightly up — misapplied pressure here scratches a radius into the frame.
If fitted, lock the slide open and install the front end of the two-piece guide rod, tightened with the 5/32 hex wrench.
fncheck: Unloaded and proven, empty magazine only, muzzle safe. Rack the slide by hand several times and feel for any catch — a tightly fitted gun should be smooth, not notchy. Check the barrel returns fully into battery every time. With the hammer cocked, apply the thumb safety: the slide should be locked and the trigger dead. Off safe, grip the pistol properly and dry-fire once; then repeat WITHOUT depressing the grip safety — the hammer must NOT fall. Finally, cycle a few dummy rounds from the magazine rather than dropping them into the chamber.
